content.text: Section 17.8 describes what the Eduversal School Appraisal does. This section explains what it is built on. It also explains why its five domains do not copy any single external framework. This matters because the appraisal often serves two audiences at once. One is an Eduversal Subject Specialist who calibrates ratings (keeps them consistent) across fifteen schools. The other is a school leader who collects evidence for CIS, WASC or BAN-S/M accreditation. Without a written mapping, the school leader has to work out the connection by eye, and every school works it out differently.

The Eduversal School Appraisal Framework deliberately combines several sources. It draws on international accreditation practice (CIS, WASC, NEASC). It draws on Cambridge's own expectations for school quality. It also draws on the Indonesian legal frameworks that bind every partner school (BAN-S/M IASP 2020 and the principal competency standards). None of these is the parent framework. Where they agree, our domains follow them. Where they differ, our domains follow what can be defended in an Indonesian Cambridge school. Sometimes that matches none of them exactly.
Keep three cautions in mind when you read the mapping tables below.

items: A mapping is a correspondence, not an equivalence. "D2 maps to WASC Category B" means that evidence collected for one can largely be used for the other. It does not mean that a strong D2 rating satisfies WASC Category B. It also does not mean that the two ask identical questions.

The mapping is many-to-many. Our five domains cover CIS's eight applicable domains (A-H) and WASC's four categories. So most of our domains answer to more than one external domain. Several external domains are also split across two of ours.

An accreditation body judges its own framework. Nothing in this section is a claim about accreditation outcomes. A school pursuing CIS or WASC still completes that body's own self-study. The appraisal reduces the work of gathering evidence; it does not replace the process.

content.text: The framework rates 33 aspects across five domains. Each aspect is rated on a 1-4 scale (1 Needs Intervention / 2 Developing / 3 Strong / 4 Outstanding). Each aspect has its own descriptor for each of the four levels. These are set out in the School Appraisal: Rating Rubric 26-27. The domains:

items: D1 — Leadership & Governance (6 aspects): vision and strategic direction, SMART goals and the P.I.E. model, leadership structure and shared leadership, performance management and staff KPIs, governance and transparent decision-making, Schoolwide Learner Outcomes

D2 — Teaching & Learning Quality (6 aspects): in-class documents and observation records, assessment methods, student understanding and goal setting, assessment and feedback quality, evaluation of teaching and PD records, LMS and technology integration

D3 — Curriculum & Academic Programs (9 aspects): department structure, department meetings and HoD coordination, teacher self-assessment, formal observations and walkthroughs, mentoring and peer observation, PD evaluation, cultural and authentic contexts, digital policy, curriculum design, coverage and progression

D4 — Student Achievement & Learning Outcomes (6 aspects): achievement data and dashboards, Olympiad resourcing and academic follow-up, Olympiad student wellbeing, support for advanced students, language support, identification of and support for extra learning needs

D5 — School Culture & Community (6 aspects): culture, climate and student behavior, safeguarding and child protection, communication structures, educational and co-curricular programs, parent and community engagement, staff wellbeing

content.text: Each domain has two Domain Leads. They keep ratings consistent across the network. The two Leads are always split across a school's two visits. So full coverage of the domain comes from the pair, not from repeat visits by one person.

editorialNotes.title: Note on the aspect count

The ninth D3 aspect — Curriculum Design, Coverage and Progression — was added to school-appraisal-framework.json on the same date, so the framework file and the published instruments (Rating Rubric, Evidence Guide, School Appraisal Handbook) now agree on 33 aspects.

content.text: CIS assesses schools against eight domains (A-H). There is also a Domain I for schools with boarding or homestay. No Eduversal partner school currently operates these (see Section 18.2 for the full list). CIS evaluation focuses on process ("how do we operate as an organization?"). Its model of a self-study followed by a peer-review visit is the structure the Eduversal appraisal follows most closely.

items: CIS Domain A (Purpose and direction) -> D1 (vision, mission, strategic planning). CIS also expects Schoolwide Learner Outcomes here; see 24.7.
CIS Domain B (Governance, ownership and leadership) -> D1 (leadership structure, governance, transparent decision-making)
CIS Domain C (The curriculum) -> D3 (curriculum delivery, departmental organization, resources)
CIS Domain D (Teaching and assessing for learning), standards D1-D6 -> D2 (classroom practice, differentiation, technology in learning)

CIS Domain D (Teaching and assessing for learning), standards D7-D8 -> D2 (assessment methods, feedback quality) and D4 (achievement data, reporting). Note: assessment is not a separate CIS domain; it sits inside Domain D.
CIS Domain E (Wellbeing) -> D5 (safeguarding, culture, behavior). Language support and extra learning needs sit in CIS Domain D (standards D4, D5) -> D4
CIS Domain F (Staffing) -> D1 (performance management) and D3 (mentoring, peer observation, PD evaluation)

CIS Domain G (Premises, facilities, technology systems and auxiliary services) -> D3 (learning resources) and D5 (facilities as they affect culture). Financial and facilities management are mostly outside our scope; see 24.8.
CIS Domain H (Community and home partnerships) -> D5 (parent and community engagement)

content.text: Eduversal takes several structural features from CIS. These are a mandatory self-study before the visit and a visiting team from outside the school. They also include commendations paired with recommendations, and a formal appeal route. Finally, there is an assigned person who gives continuity. The CIS Visiting Team Leader is the model for our Visit I Supervisor.

subsections.title: WASC — ACS WASC Focus on Learning

content.text: The WASC framework that applies to partner schools is the ACS WASC "Focus on Learning" (FOL) model for K-12 schools. It is not the Postsecondary framework, which applies to colleges and universities. FOL focuses more on outcomes than CIS does: it asks what impact school practices have on student learning. It has four categories, plus the schoolwide action plan as a required deliverable:

items: Category A Organization for Student Learning -> D1 (vision, governance, leadership, resource alignment)
Category B Curriculum, Instruction, and Assessment -> D2 and D3 (standards-based curriculum, instructional quality, assessment systems, use of data)
Category C Support for Student Personal and Academic Growth -> D4 (language support, extra learning needs, advanced students) and D5 (pastoral care, wellbeing)
Category D Resource Management and Development -> partially D3 (learning resources) and D5 (facilities, staff wellbeing). Financial resourcing is out of scope; see 24.8.

The WASC schoolwide action plan (Chapter V of the self-study, linked to Task 5 - a deliverable, not a category) -> the appraisal's own action-plan cycle. A school rated Needs Intervention must produce a mandatory action plan within four weeks. The school's Visit I Supervisor follows up progress in the Follow-up Sessions they lead. Progress is also followed up at the Phase 4 Impact Review in May–June, and in the following cycle.

content.text: Eduversal takes two things from WASC. The first is the model of a self-study that a visiting committee then validates. The second is the discipline of judging practices by their effect on learning, not by whether they exist on paper. WASC separates a Focus Visit (quality of teaching) from a Full Visit (the whole institutional system). This is the model for splitting our cycle into a Phase 1 Teaching Quality Visit and a Phase 3 Validation Visit.

editorialNotes.text: Corrected 2026-09-30: this previously placed the review at a Phase 2 mid-year check-in; in the live cycle Phase 2 is the Progress Check-in held between the Phase 1 and Phase 3 visits, before Domain Ratings are set

content.text: NEASC's ACE (Accreditation for Curriculum Effectiveness) model rates schools against learner-centered principles, not compliance checklists. Eduversal takes one specific idea from it. A judgment of quality must reach the student's actual experience of learning, not stop at the systems meant to produce it.

items: ACE learning principles -> D4 (Student Achievement & Learning Outcomes), which carries this idea most directly. This is why D4 is a separate domain and not a sub-section of D2
ACE foundation standards -> D1 (governance and strategic direction) and D5 (culture and community as the conditions for learning)
The NEASC School Liaison Officer manages the self-study relationship across the cycle. This role is a second example behind our paired supervisor model

subsections.title: Indonesian Frameworks — IASP 2020 and Principal Competency Standards

content.text: BAN-S/M (Badan Akreditasi Nasional Sekolah/Madrasah) is the national accreditation body for schools. It accredits Indonesian schools against the IASP 2020 instrument (Instrumen Akreditasi Satuan Pendidikan). Unlike CIS and WASC, this accreditation is not optional. It is the legal accreditation framework. Partner schools are subject to it whatever their Cambridge status. IASP 2020 has four components:

items: Mutu Lulusan (graduate quality) -> D4 (achievement data, learning outcomes) and D5 (student behavior and character)
Proses Pembelajaran (learning process) -> D2 (classroom practice, assessment, feedback)
Mutu Guru (teacher quality) -> D2 (evaluation of teaching) and D3 (PD, mentoring, peer observation, department structures)
Manajemen Sekolah (school management) -> D1 (leadership, governance, performance management) and D5 (communication, parent engagement)

content.text: In practice, the evidence collected for an Eduversal appraisal is largely the evidence an IASP visit asks for. So the Phase 3 Validation Visit can be run as an IASP-readiness audit. The reverse is not true. IASP does not ask about Cambridge program implementation, Olympiad provision or EAL (English as an Additional Language) support as deeply as D3 and D4 require.
Indonesian competency standards (PMD) are linked to the appraisal domains. This way, staff development and school appraisal connect with each other instead of running as unrelated judgments.

Safeguarding in D5 follows Permendikdasmen 6/2026 (Budaya Sekolah Aman dan Nyaman, a safe and comfortable school culture). This regulation revoked Permendikbudristek 46/2023 PPKSP on 9 January 2026. SPK schools that run Cambridge are covered by it. See Section 9 for the operational detail. Note two points about 6/2026 in particular. It makes the kepala sekolah (principal) the single accountable officer. It also sets no legal deadline for reporting.

editorialNotes.text:
Indonesian competency standards are carried on the appraisal domains as PMD tags, so that staff development and school appraisal cross-walk rather than running as unrelated judgments.

NOTE a known inconsistency here, flagged 2026-07-29 and not yet resolved: the PMD chip family resolves against Permendiknas No. 16/2007 (Standar Kualifikasi Akademik dan Kompetensi Guru — the four TEACHER pillars: pedagogik, profesional, sosial, kepribadian), and the frameworkAnchors on D2/D3/D4 tag those teacher pillars.

But D1 and D5 tag 'Kompetensi Manajerial', 'Kompetensi Kewirausahaan' and 'Kompetensi Sosial' / 'Kepribadian', which belong to Permendiknas No. 13/2007 (Standar Kepala Sekolah/Madrasah — the five PRINCIPAL competencies).

The two regulations are being tagged under one chip family, and 13/2007 is not in the research archive, so the manajerial and kewirausahaan chips currently resolve to nothing.

items: Currently tagged, resolving via 16/2007 (teacher pillars): Kompetensi Pedagogik -> D2, D3 · Kompetensi Profesional -> D2, D3, D4 · Kompetensi Sosial -> D5 · Kompetensi Kepribadian -> D5
Currently tagged, NOT resolving (13/2007 principal competencies, absent from the archive): Kompetensi Manajerial -> D1 · Kompetensi Kewirausahaan -> D1
Not tagged anywhere: Kompetensi Supervisi (13/2007), which would map naturally to D2 and D3

Resolution requires a decision: either archive 13/2007 and split PMD into two chip families (teacher vs principal), or drop the principal competencies from the appraisal tags and carry them only on principal appraisal. Do not silently rewrite the tags to fit the existing chip family — that would hide a real gap in the Indonesian legal mapping.

content.text: Cambridge International publishes a school self-evaluation expectation. It also publishes the Cambridge School Leader Standards (CSLS 2023, 25 standards across 5 areas). CSLS references are given for every appraisal domain. This means a leadership development conversation and a school appraisal rating point at the same standard, not at two different vocabularies.

Cambridge program implementation (syllabus coverage, centre obligations, exam administration) is assessed through D3. However, the authoritative detail is in Sections 3 and 10, not in the appraisal framework.
The mapping is open about its limits. Four differences are deliberate. Any school that uses the appraisal to prepare for accreditation should be told about them.

items: Schoolwide Learner Outcomes. Both CIS and WASC put SLOs at the center. WASC's whole FOL model is organized around them. The appraisal includes an explicit SLO aspect (D1-a6), so it prompts schools to address them. A school preparing for CIS or WASC will be asked whether its SLOs are defined, mapped into the curriculum and backed by evidence. The aspect asks whether SLOs exist and work. It does not write them for the school.

Financial and facilities management. CIS Domain G and WASC Category D both assess financial sustainability, facilities and resourcing as part of institutional quality. The Eduversal appraisal has an academic scope. It covers resources only where they affect teaching (D3) or culture (D5). Governance of finance sits with the Yayasan and is outside the appraisal.

Cycle length and independence. CIS and WASC run multi-year cycles, with teams drawn from independent peer schools. The Eduversal cycle is annual, and the team comes from the network's own specialists. This is a considered trade-off. It gives frequency, subject expertise and continuity. The cost is the external independence that an accreditation body requires. The appraisal is internal quality assurance, not a simulation of accreditation. From AY 2026-2027 the network also runs Network Learning Visits. In these visits, two leaders from one partner school spend a day at another school (see clause 18.8). These visits do not close this gap and must not be presented as closing it. For an accreditation body, independence means a visitor with no stake in the outcome, trained and sent by the accreditor. A network peer is neither. The visits carry no rating and produce nothing that enters the appraisal record. They are professional learning, not an independent review team.

Outcome type. Accreditation gives a yes-or-no decision (accredited or not). The appraisal gives a Development Rating for each domain. This rating is explicitly a development indicator, not a ranking. There is no single composite school score. A school rated Developing is not "failing accreditation". It has named priorities and a supervisor assigned to them.

content.text: Where a school is actively working toward CIS or WASC accreditation, Section 18 (Accreditation Toolkit) governs. This section explains how appraisal evidence feeds into that process. It does not replace the accreditation body's own self-study instrument.

The original text stated that review teams are drawn from the network’s own specialists rather than from peer schools; that remains true of the appraisal, and the extension records what the new visits are and — more importantly — what they are not. The count of four divergences is unchanged.

Schoolwide Learner Outcomes. Both CIS and WASC place SLOs at the centre — WASC's entire FOL model is organized around them. Eduversal added an explicit SLO aspect (D1-a6) on 2026-07-29, so the appraisal now prompts for them; a school preparing for CIS or WASC will be asked whether its SLOs are defined, mapped into curriculum, and evidenced. The aspect asks whether SLOs exist and work — it does not author them for the school.

The published appraisal instruments (Rating Rubric, Evidence Guide, School Appraisal Handbook) are the source of truth for the framework's content; school-appraisal-framework.json is the runtime copy and must match them, and this section is the narrative description of both. If this section and the JSON disagree, correct whichever one has drifted from the published instruments — neither wins automatically. (Revised 2026-08-20: the old rule made this section the source of truth and required the JSON to follow it on any disagreement. Applied literally, that rule ordered a framework change nobody had decided. On the same date the JSON was aligned to the instruments by adding the ninth D3 aspect, Curriculum Design — D3 now has 9 aspects and the framework 33 in total.)

When the appraisal framework changes (a domain renamed, an aspect added or retired), update 24.2 and re-check every mapping table. The framework's own file is Central Hub/resources/school-appraisal-framework.json, mirrored byte-identically into Academic Hub.

editorialNotes.title: Maintenance of this section (for Eduversal editors)
editorialNotes.text:
This section is a mapping between documents that change independently, so it goes stale silently. Three maintenance rules:
- When the appraisal framework changes (a domain renamed, an aspect added or retired), update 24.2 and re-check every mapping table.
- When an external framework publishes a new edition, verify the mapping before changing the edition number. A new CIS or WASC edition can renumber or merge domains, which silently invalidates rows here.
- The published appraisal instruments (Rating Rubric, Evidence Guide, School Appraisal Handbook) are the source of truth for the framework's content; this section describes them.
